title: Window to acquit Maria Ressa

Three rebuttals CJ argues should have been raised on the stand: (1) fair comment on public-interest matter; (2) government weaponization of cybercrime law to harass/intimidate/silence Rappler; (3) sufficient reasons for seven-month refusal to publish Keng's side

stances.claim: The Manila RTC and the Court of Appeals (CA decision penned by J Roberto P. Quiroz, concurred in by JJ Bato and Legaspi) correctly found Ressa and Santos guilty of cyberlibel given the evidence: the Feb. 19, 2014 Rappler republication 'maliciously and publicly branded' Wilfredo Keng as 'human trafficker, a drug and contraband smuggler, and worst, a murderer'; Keng was never charged with those crimes; he is a private citizen so malice is presumed by law; the burden to rebut shifted to the accused; and 'lamentably, the defense miserably failed.'

Beyond the presumed-malice burden, lower courts found 'actual, not just presumed malice' -- yet 'oddly, both accused did not take the witness stand to contest this point and to explain their defenses.' Their three available rebuttals -- fair comment on public-interest matter; government weaponization of cybercrime law to 'harass, intimidate and silence' Rappler; and sufficient reasons for the seven-month refusal to publish Keng's side -- were aired in 'public fora and the media' rather than courtroom testimony, but 'courts do not base their rulings on media reports and public assemblies.'

The 'window' to acquittal on SC appeal lies in the 'truly viable defense' Ressa and Santos should have raised by skipping the CA and going directly to the SC: the crime has prescribed because the one-year libel prescriptive period had lapsed when the DOJ filed the charge. The CA was bound by Tolentino v. People (Aug. 6, 2018), an unsigned resolution setting cyberlibel prescription at 15 years -- and only the SC en banc can reverse or modify Tolentino.

Santos's reconciliatory response ('the rule of law will prevail') and Ressa's bitter response ('Philippine legal system is not doing enough') diverge sharply. CJ hopes 'the high court justices will rise above the emotional outbursts' and 'would -- like me if I were still an incumbent -- veer toward the one-year prescriptive period because, philosophically, I believe that society is better served when cases are filed and prosecuted speedily.'

By defending themselves with all available legal weapons, both accused 'have shown their trust in our judicial system; thus, they should accept whatever may be the final decision of the highest court' -- otherwise they should have refused to participate in the proceedings from the start, as Sen. Benigno Aquino Jr. did when he was tried by a military tribunal that 'subsequently sentenced him to death.'
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-of-law-acceptance principle with historical Aquino precedent

notable_anecdotes: The 37-page RTC decision detail -- making concrete the lower-court production CJ characterizes as 'carefully crafted.'
The verbatim DOJ-charge language -- 'human trafficker, a drug and contraband smuggler, and worst, a murderer' -- preserved as the imputation that triggered the libel finding.
The seven-month Rappler refusal to publish Keng's side 'despite numerous follow-up' -- concrete fact-pattern detail that undermines the fair-comment defense if not affirmatively rebutted.
CJ's diagnostic 'Oddly, both accused did not take the witness stand' -- the procedural choice CJ identifies as decisive for the lower-courts' rulings.
The Tolentino v. People unsigned-resolution detail -- making explicit the precedent that binds the CA and identifying the specific institutional handoff (en banc only) needed to dislodge it.

Santos's quoted reconciliatory line -- 'the rule of law will prevail' -- contrasted with Ressa's bitter quoted line about the 'Philippine legal system' -- modeling the two responses for SC justices to read.
CJ's hypothetical incumbency self-positioning -- 'like me if I were still an incumbent' -- rare counterfactual disclosure of how he would rule, transparent about his philosophical leaning.

The Sen. Aquino Jr. precedent -- refusing to participate before a military tribunal that 'subsequently sentenced him to death' -- used as the moral exemplar of forum-rejection-as-principled-protest, the contrapositive of Ressa's participation.

The 'speedy filing and prosecution' philosophy disclosure -- anchoring CJ's prescriptive lean toward the one-year prescriptive period in a substantive jurisprudential preference rather than personal sympathy.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the path forward for multi-awarded Rappler CEO Maria Ressa and former Rappler staffer Reynaldo Santos Jr. after the Court of Appeals' October 10, 2022 denial of their motion for reconsideration of the CA's earlier judgment (penned by Justice Roberto P. Quiroz, concurred in by Justices Ramon M. Bato Jr. and Germano Francisco D. Legaspi) affirming the 37-page Manila RTC decision finding them guilty of cyberlibel. The Department of Justice charged that on or about February 19, 2014, the accused re-published a Rappler article that 'maliciously and publicly branded' Wilfredo Keng -- a private citizen -- 'as a human trafficker, a drug and contraband smuggler, and worst, a murderer.' Libel under the Revised Penal Code requires public and malicious imputation of a crime/vice/defect causing dishonor via printed media; the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 extended this to 'computer system or any other similar means' and increased the penalty. Keng was never charged with the imputed crimes; because he is a private citizen, malice is presumed by law and the burden to rebut shifted to the accused -- and 'lamentably, the defense miserably failed.' Worse, the lower courts found 'actual,' not just 'presumed,' malice. 'Oddly, both accused did not take the witness stand to contest this point and to explain their defenses.' In past pieces, CJ had opined they should have testified to show that (1) the republished article was fair comment on a matter of public interest, (2) the government weaponized the cybercrime law to 'harass, intimidate and silence' them and Rappler, and (3) Rappler had sufficient reasons for its seven-month refusal to publish Keng's side. Instead they aired their defenses in 'the public fora and the media' -- but 'courts do not base their rulings on media reports and public assemblies.' He had also opined that after the trial court's decision, they should have skipped the CA and appealed directly to the SC to raise their 'truly viable defense' -- that the crime had prescribed because the one-year libel prescriptive period had lapsed when the DOJ filed the charge. The CA was bound by Tolentino v. People (August 6, 2018), an unsigned resolution setting cyberlibel prescription at 15 years; only the Supreme Court en banc can reverse or modify that resolution. Santos was reconciliatory after the MR denial -- 'not surprising but disheartening, nevertheless... we still believe that the rule of law will prevail' -- but Ressa was bitter: 'Philippine legal system is not doing enough to stop it. I am disappointed by today's ruling but sadly not surprised.' Ignoring Ressa's bitterness, CJ hopes the high court justices 'will rise above the emotional outbursts' and 'would -- like me if I were still an incumbent -- veer toward the one-year prescriptive period because, philosophically, I believe that society is better served when cases are filed and prosecuted speedily.' He closes on a rule-of-law principle: by defending themselves with all available legal weapons, both accused 'have shown their trust in our judicial system; thus, they should accept whatever may be the final decision of the highest court. Otherwise, they should have refused to participate in the judicial proceedings from the very beginning like what former senator Benigno Aquino Jr. did when he was tried by a military tribunal that subsequently sentenced him to death.'
